3. Training Versus Inference

blocks.alt: Training updates weights while inference uses fixed weights

blocks.text: This connects back to training and its own loss functions, already covered generally across this course. Training genuinely adjusts a model's own weights; inference genuinely uses those already-fixed weights instead.
No genuinely further learning happens during inference: the weights genuinely stay completely frozen, a genuinely fundamental distinction explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 4. The Forward Pass At Inference Time
This connects back to training versus inference, already covered in this topic. A prompt's own tokens genuinely flow through the entire network in one single forward pass.
This produces genuinely one probability distribution over the vocabulary, already covered generally in Sampling, the exact starting point for choosing the very next token.
5. Inference Is Repeated Per Token

blocks.alt: Token 1, 2, and 3 are each produced by a repeated inference step

blocks.text: This connects back to the forward pass at inference time, already covered in this topic. Generating genuinely more than one token genuinely requires running that forward pass once per new token.
Each genuinely new token gets appended, and the entire process genuinely repeats, already covered generally in Sampling, a genuinely repeated cost explored throughout the rest of this topic.
6. Recapping KV Caching

blocks.alt: Past keys and values are cached and reused each step

blocks.text: This connects back to inference being repeated per token, already covered in this topic. Recomputing genuinely every earlier token's own attention values at every single step is genuinely wasteful.

Caching genuinely those earlier computed values lets each genuinely new step reuse them instead of redoing all that work, a genuinely important optimization explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.content: This caching technique, already covered in this topic, directly explains why generation typically gets noticeably faster after the very first token, since later steps genuinely reuse work already done earlier.

blocks.text: 7. Latency And Throughput

blocks.alt: Latency measures time per request while throughput measures requests per second

blocks.text: This connects back to inference being repeated per token, already covered in this topic. Latency genuinely measures how long one single generation call takes.
Throughput genuinely measures how many separate requests a system can genuinely serve at once, a genuinely distinct, complementary metric explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 8. Batching Inference Requests

blocks.alt: Request 1 and request 2 are batched together

blocks.text: This connects back to latency and throughput, already covered in this topic. Genuinely serving many separate requests together in one batch genuinely improves overall throughput.
This often happens at the genuine cost of slightly higher latency for any one genuinely individual request, a genuinely real tradeoff explored throughout the rest of this topic.
9. Recognizing Why Inference Is Genuinely Treated As Its Own Distinct Engineering Problem

blocks.alt: Serving models at scale points toward optimizing inference separately

blocks.text: This connects back to training versus inference, already covered in this topic. Inference, already covered in this topic, genuinely runs continuously in production, unlike one-time training.

This connects back to a genuinely simple, direct next-token strategy, already covered generally in Sampling. Temperature, covered as the next topic in this module, genuinely refines exactly that strategy.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates the repeated, per-token inference loop, already covered in this topic, generating a few tokens step by step.

code.content:
import random
random.seed(0)

def forward_pass(prompt_tokens):
    # already covered as the forward pass at inference time in this topic
    # simplified: returns a fake probability distribution over a tiny vocabulary
    vocabulary = ["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "mat", "."]
    weights = [random.uniform(0.1, 1.0) for _ in vocabulary]
    return vocabulary, weights

def generate(prompt_tokens, max_new_tokens=4):
    # already covered as inference being repeated per token in this topic
    generated = list(prompt_tokens)
    for step in range(max_new_tokens):
        vocabulary, weights = forward_pass(generated)
        next_token = random.choices(vocabulary, weights=weights, k=1)[0]
        generated.append(next_token)
        print(f"  step {step + 1} (already covered as one forward pass per token in this topic): generated so far = {generated}")
    return generated

prompt = ["the"]
print(f"Prompt (already covered generally in Prompting): {prompt}")
final_output = generate(prompt)
print(f"\nFinal generated sequence: {final_output}")

blocks.content: Running this example shows one new token being generated at each step, with the running sequence growing by exactly one token per forward pass, exactly the repeated inference loop already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Inference is the runtime process that turns a prompt into a real, generated response.
Training adjusts a model's weights; inference uses those already-fixed, frozen weights instead.
A prompt's tokens flow through the network in one forward pass, producing a probability distribution.
Generating more than one token requires running that forward pass once per new token.
Caching earlier computed attention values avoids wastefully recomputing them at every step.
Latency measures how long one generation call takes; throughput measures requests served overall.
Batching requests together improves throughput, often at the cost of slightly higher individual latency.
Inference runs continuously in production, making it its own distinct engineering problem.
